“Let’s be the same wound if we must bleed. Let’s fight side by side, even if the enemy is ourselves: I am yours, you are mine.” —Tommy Olofsson, Sweden I’m not interested in who suffered the most. I’m interested in people getting over it. Once when my father was a boy a stone hit him on the head. Hair would never grow there. Our fingers found the tender spot and its riddle: the boy who has fallen stands up. A bucket of pears in his mother’s doorway welcomes him home. The pears are not crying. Later his friend who threw the stone says he was aiming at a bird. And my father starts growing wings. Each carries a tender spot: something our lives forgot to give us. A man builds a house and says, “I am native now.” A woman speaks to a tree in place of her son. And olives come. A child’s poem says, “I don’t like wars, they end up with monuments.” He’s painting a bird with wings wide enough to cover two roofs at once. Why are we so monumentally slow? Soldiers stalk a pharmacy: big guns, little pills. If you tilt your head just slightly it’s ridiculous. There’s a place in my brain where hate won’t grow. I touch its riddle: wind, and seeds. Something pokes us as we sleep. It’s late but everything comes next.

Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Let, Tommy, Olofsson

outputs.L1:
“Let’s be the same wound if we must bleed. Let’s fight side by side, even if the enemy is ourselves: I am yours, you are mine.”  
—Tommy Olofsson, Sweden

I’m not interested in who suffered the most. I’m interested in people getting over it.

Once, when my father was a boy, a stone hit him on the head. Hair would never grow there. Our fingers found the tender spot and its riddle: the boy who has fallen stands up. A bucket of pears in his mother’s doorway welcomes him home. The pears are not crying. Later, his friend who threw the stone says he was aiming at a bird. And my father starts growing wings.

Each of us carries a tender spot: something our lives forgot to give us. A man builds a house and says, “I am native now.” A woman speaks to a tree in place of her son. And olives come.

A child’s poem says, “I don’t like wars; they end up with monuments.” He’s painting a bird with wings wide enough to cover two roofs at once. Why are we so monumentally slow?

Soldiers stalk a pharmacy: big guns, little pills. If you tilt your head just slightly, it’s ridiculous.

There’s a place in my brain where hate won’t grow. I touch its riddle: wind, and seeds. Something pokes us as we sleep. It’s late, but everything comes next.
outputs.L2:
“If bleeding is unavoidable, let it be from one shared hurt. Let us stand together in struggle, even when what we battle is within us: I belong to you, and you belong to me.” —Tommy Olofsson, Sweden

I do not care to measure whose pain was greater. What matters to me is how people move beyond it.

When my father was young, a rock struck his head. Hair never returned to that place. Our hands would search out that sensitive patch and the question it carried: the child who was knocked down gets back on his feet. At his mother’s entrance, a pail filled with pears waits to greet him. The pears shed no tears.

Years afterward, the friend who had thrown the rock explains that he had meant to hit a bird. And then my father begins to sprout wings.

Everyone bears a sore place: some absence life failed to provide. A man puts up a home and declares, “Now I belong here.” A woman talks to a tree as though it were her son. Then olives appear.

In a child’s poem, the child writes, “I don’t like wars; they finish by becoming monuments.” He is drawing a bird whose outstretched wings are broad enough to shelter two rooftops at the same time.

Why do we take so impossibly long to understand?

Soldiers prowl around a pharmacy: enormous weapons, tiny medicines. Turn your head a little, and the scene becomes absurd.

Inside my mind there is a place where hatred cannot take root. I put my hand to its mystery: air moving, seeds waiting.

Something nudges us while we are sleeping. The hour is late, but everything is still ahead.
outputs.L3:
The speaker places greater value on healing and moving forward than on measuring or comparing suffering. Rather than asking who has endured the worst pain, the poem turns attention toward recovery, compassion, and the possibility of continuing life after loss. This perspective suggests that suffering should not become a competition. Instead, shared pain can become a reason to understand one another more deeply.

The poem also suggests that every person carries a “tender spot,” a hidden wound shaped by what life has failed to give them. This wound may come from loss, disappointment, violence, exile, or the absence of love and safety. By describing this private vulnerability, the poem reminds us that pain is often invisible. People may appear strong on the outside while still carrying memories or longings that remain sensitive and unresolved.

Throughout the poem, natural images such as pears, wings, trees, olives, and birds point toward resilience and renewal. These images suggest growth, nourishment, movement, and freedom. Trees and olives are especially associated with endurance, rootedness, and peace, while wings and birds evoke the possibility of escape, hope, and new beginnings. Even in a world marked by suffering, these images show that life continues to offer signs of beauty and restoration.

At the same time, the poem strongly criticizes war as absurd and destructive. This criticism is especially powerful when seen through the perspective of a child, who understands war as something that ends in monuments. The child’s view exposes the emptiness of war’s supposed glory: after violence and death, what remains are memorials to those who were lost. In this way, the poem questions the purpose of war and highlights its tragic consequences.

Ultimately, the speaker insists that hate does not have to take root in the human heart. Although pain can leave lasting wounds, it does not have to produce bitterness or revenge. The poem offers a vision in which hope can still grow after suffering, just as trees can grow from damaged ground. By choosing healing over hatred, the speaker affirms the possibility of peace, renewal, and a more compassionate future.
outputs.L4:
Inherited wounds do not belong only to the bodies that first received them. They pass from hand to hand, from parent to child, through stories told at kitchen tables, through silences at funerals, through names carved into stone and names never spoken again. A scar can become a family heirloom. A memory can become a border. Long after the shelling stops, people may still carry the sound of it inside them, hearing it in a slammed door, in a sudden cry, in the quiet before dawn.

In times of conflict, suffering is often measured as though pain were a contest. One side counts its graves, the other its ruins. One person points to a missing brother, another to a burned home, another to a childhood spent under fear. But grief cannot be weighed fairly against grief. No scale can decide which mother wept more honestly, which wound deserves the greater witness, which hunger was more holy. To compare suffering is to misunderstand it. Pain does not become smaller because someone else has suffered too; it only becomes lonelier when it is used as a weapon.

War enters ordinary life not only through violence, but through the way it changes daily gestures. Bread is baked beside cracked windows. Children learn the routes that avoid danger before they learn the names of birds. Lovers whisper under curfew. Old men sweep dust from doorways that may be broken again tomorrow. A woman folds laundry while listening for sirens. A boy keeps a photograph in his pocket until the corners soften and the faces blur. Even in devastation, life insists on continuing, but it continues with a limp.

The deepest injury of war may be the temptation to inherit hatred along with sorrow. People are taught whom to fear, whom to blame, whose dead to mourn and whose to ignore. The past becomes a room with no windows, crowded with ghosts demanding loyalty. Yet reconciliation begins when someone refuses to add another stone to the wall. It begins when a person looks across a line of anger and recognizes not an enemy, but another human being carrying their own ashes, their own torn letters, their own unhealed names.

Healing does not mean forgetting. It does not ask the wounded to pretend that nothing happened, or to forgive before they are ready, or to replace justice with politeness. True healing honors memory without allowing memory to harden into cruelty. It makes room for mourning, for truth, for accountability, and also for the fragile possibility that the future need not repeat the past. It understands that tenderness is not weakness. In a world trained by violence, tenderness is an act of resistance.

Peace, then, is more than the absence of war. It is the rebuilding of trust in small, human ways: sharing water, opening a door, listening without interrupting, burying the dead with dignity, teaching children a song that does not ask them to hate. It is found in hands that choose to plant instead of strike, in neighbors who sit together after years of suspicion, in the courage to say, “Your grief is real, and so is mine.”

Monuments to pain may preserve memory, but they cannot by themselves heal the living. Stone can name the dead, but it cannot hold a frightened child. Bronze can mark a battlefield, but it cannot teach mercy. The more meaningful memorial is a life no longer governed by vengeance: a table where former enemies share bread, a street where children walk without fear, a language in which sorrow is not used to summon more sorrow.

The text ultimately suggests that the way forward is not through the ranking of wounds, nor through the worship of suffering, but through a shared tenderness that refuses hatred its inheritance. When people choose to recognize one another’s humanity, even amid the ruins, they begin to loosen the grip of the past. Peace becomes not an abstract ideal, but a daily practice: humble, difficult, and profoundly brave. It is in that choice—to care despite memory, to reach despite injury—that healing begins.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem about inherited trauma, reconciliation, and war, beginning with a quote attributed to Tommy Olofsson of Sweden and using images of pears, stones, birds, olives, soldiers, and monuments.
counterfactuals.output:
“Something in us remembers what we have never lived.” — Tommy Olofsson, Sweden

The pear tree leaned over the yard as if listening to the house breathe in its sleep. Every autumn its fruit fell bruised into the grass, yellow-green and soft as old apologies, and my grandmother gathered them in her apron without saying the names of the dead. She had learned that silence could be peeled with a knife, sliced thin, served on a blue plate beside bread and olives. She had learned that a table could hold a family together even when history sat among us like a stone no one could lift.

There were stones everywhere: in the fields, in the walls, in the pockets of boys who became soldiers before their voices had finished changing. Stones in the mouths of fathers. Stones on the graves of strangers. Stones stacked into monuments in the square, where bronze men raised bronze rifles toward a sky that never answered. We passed them on our way to market, carrying pears, carrying oil, carrying the small stubborn errands of peace. The monuments had names, but not all the names. The wind knew the rest.

War arrived before I did, yet it had already furnished my childhood. It slept in the cupboard with the chipped cups. It hid in my mother’s flinch when a door slammed. It darkened the stories that stopped at the edge of a sentence, where someone would look out the window and say, The birds are back. And they were: swallows stitching the evening together, crows arguing in the olives, sparrows bathing in dust as if dust were a kind of mercy. Their wings wrote what we could not: departure, return, departure.

I inherited no uniform, only the trembling after. No medal, only the way hunger made my grandfather count each pear before giving it away. No battlefield, only the map of fear folded into the body and passed from hand to hand like a family photograph. Still, I carried it. We all carried it. Even love, in our house, wore boots at first.

But reconciliation began quietly, not with trumpets, not beneath monuments, but under the pear tree when my mother placed a stone in my palm and said, This was from the road your grandfather walked home on. It was warm from the sun, ordinary, almost weightless. For the first time I understood: what is inherited can also be set down. Not forgotten. Set down.

So we laid stones at the roots. We pressed olives into oil. We fed the birds through winter. We spoke the names we knew and left room for those we did not. The soldiers in the square remained bronze, but the children climbed their pedestals and laughed, and the laughter rose, irreverent and bright, into the same sky.

When the pears ripened again, we ate them whole, juice running down our wrists like a blessing no war had managed to cancel.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a Naomi Shihab Nye–style meditation on conflict and healing, with a personal anecdote about a father struck by a stone as a child and a hopeful ending about hate not growing.
counterfactuals.output:
I can’t write in Naomi Shihab Nye’s exact style, but here is an original lyrical meditation on conflict and healing, with a gentle, reflective spirit:

---

My father once told me about the stone.

He was a boy then, small enough that the world still arrived at him from above: adults’ hands, windowsills, the branches of trees, the loud opinions of men. He was walking home when another child threw it. Not a pebble, not an accident, but a stone chosen for its weight.

It struck him near the eye.

For years, he carried the story quietly, the way some people carry a scar beneath a sleeve. He did not make a monument of it. He did not teach us to hate the boy who threw it. He only said, “It hurt,” and then he went on slicing apples, fixing the loose hinge, turning the radio down when the news became too much.

I have thought often about that restraint.

How easy it would have been to place the stone on the family table and say: Here. This is what the world is. This is what they did. Remember it. Pass it on.

But he did not pass it on.

Or rather, he passed on something else: the knowledge of pain without the command to multiply it. The memory of injury without the permission to become cruel.

Conflict begins, sometimes, with a hand closing around a stone. Healing begins when another hand opens.

Not all wounds disappear. Some become weather. Some become the careful way a person listens when someone else is afraid. Some become the refusal to laugh at another child’s tears. My father’s wound did not make him soft in the way people misunderstand softness. It made him strong enough not to throw back every hard thing that had been thrown at him.

This is not the same as forgetting.

The stone happened. The bruise bloomed. The child went home changed.

But hate, too, needs tending. It needs to be watered, repeated, named as inheritance. It needs a chair pulled up for it at dinner, a bed made for it in the next generation.

My father gave it no room.

And because of that, something ended with him. Or maybe something began: a small clearing, a place where children could stand without being handed the old stones.

I believe in that clearing.

I believe the heart can remember and still remain uncolonized by bitterness. I believe a story can be told without becoming a weapon. I believe a child struck by a stone can grow into a man who teaches his children, quietly and every day, that pain is real—but it is not the only thing that can be passed down.

Somewhere, the stone is gone.

The hand is empty.

The hate does not grow.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poetic essay that argues against comparing suffering, focusing instead on people getting over wounds, using surreal but gentle imagery and references to war, family memory, and peace.
counterfactuals.output:
There is no scale delicate enough to weigh a wound against another wound.

Set one grief on the left pan: a city shelled until its windows become mouths of dust. Set another on the right: a child at a kitchen table, hearing for the first time that someone they loved will not come home. The scale trembles, ashamed of itself. The needle does not know where to point. Pain is not grain or gold. It cannot be measured into sacks, cannot be auctioned, cannot be made obedient by numbers.

And yet we are tempted. We say: this sorrow is larger, that sorrow is smaller. We arrange human hurt like soldiers on a map, rank after rank, as if the heart were a battlefield with tidy borders. But suffering does not wear a uniform. It slips through trenches, through nursery curtains, through the sleeves of old coats hanging in family closets. It hides in medals and in teacups. It speaks in the silence between a grandmother’s stories, when she pauses before naming the village that no longer exists.

My grandfather never described the war in full. He offered it in fragments, like bread broken for birds: a winter road, a horse standing without a rider, the strange kindness of a stranger who shared a cigarette under a sky bruised purple by planes. My mother remembered him waking at night, not screaming, only sitting up as if he had heard a train arrive inside the walls. No one in the family called this heroic. No one called it small. It simply remained: a dark fish moving beneath the floorboards of memory.

Beside it were other hurts. A sister who buried her first child. An uncle who laughed too loudly because silence frightened him. A cousin who survived a house where love had thorns. Which pain deserved the tallest candle? Which grief had earned the right to be called real? The questions themselves were cruel little machines. They made people stand in line for compassion, holding out their scars like papers at a checkpoint.

But wounds do not need comparison. They need tending.

A wound asks for clean water, not a courtroom. It asks for hands that do not flinch. It asks for time, though time is not a doctor so much as a field where the body learns again how to grow grass over burnt places. Healing is rarely triumphant. It is not a trumpet over the ruins. More often it is a bowl of soup placed quietly in front of someone who has forgotten hunger. It is a letter answered after months. It is the first night without the old dream. It is a veteran planting tomatoes with the same hands that once shook in foxholes. It is a mother folding a dead child’s blanket and still opening the window for spring.

To get over a wound does not mean to abandon it. We do not climb grief like a wall and drop it behind us. We carry it differently. At first it is a stone in the chest; later, perhaps, a stone in the pocket; later still, a smooth stone held sometimes in the palm, warmed by the living hand. The scar remains, but it becomes less of a border and more of a weather mark, saying: here the storm passed through, and here, impossibly, the house still stands.

Peace begins in this refusal to rank pain.

Wars are born, in part, from the old arithmetic of injury: our dead matter more than yours, our tears are purer, our history is the only history with blood in it. Nations teach their children to count graves selectively. Families do it too, in quieter rooms. One person says, “You think that was bad?” and another person’s heart folds itself smaller. Thus the world rehearses violence at the dinner table before it ever reaches the frontier.

What if, instead, we taught another language?

What if we said: your wound is not my wound, but I will sit beside you while it rains. What if we believed that sorrow could be different without becoming unequal? The widow and the refugee, the lonely child and the exhausted nurse, the son of a soldier and the daughter of an enemy soldier—all carry rooms inside them where something broke. We do not need to decide whose room is darkest. We need to bring lamps.

Imagine a peace conference held not in a marble hall but in an orchard after rain. The generals arrive with maps, but the maps unfold into tablecloths. The borders turn into blue veins of rivers. Someone’s grandmother pours tea for everyone, even the translator, even the man who cannot stop crying. In the branches above them, white birds hang like folded letters. No one is asked to prove their suffering. No one is told it was not enough. They speak of the dead, then of bread, then of how to rebuild the bridge.

This is not innocence. It is discipline. Gentleness is not forgetting the war; it is refusing to let the war become the shape of every thought. It is the courage to stop polishing old bullets into family heirlooms. It is the decision to lay the rifle down in the mind, again and again, until the mind grows flowers over it.

We inherit more than pain. We inherit songs hummed while peeling potatoes, recipes written in fading ink, the names of rivers, the stubborn joke told at every funeral. We inherit the memory of people who endured, not so that we might compete in endurance, but so that we might continue the unfinished labor of tenderness. Our ancestors do not ask us to make monuments of our wounds. They ask, if they ask anything, that we learn how to live without passing the blade forward.

So let us stop comparing suffering. Let us stop building ladders from bones. Let us admit that every grief is a country with its own weather, its own moon, its own untranslatable birds. Then let us become travelers of mercy, arriving without flags, carrying bandages, soup, silence, and seeds.

The world is full of people getting over wounds—not always by being cured, not always by being whole, but by waking, washing their faces, opening the door, and letting morning touch what still hurts. There is a peace in that. Not the peace of untouched fields, but the peace of fields after battle, where poppies rise like small red lanterns and the earth, having swallowed so much iron, chooses again to grow wheat.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an original free-verse poem inspired by Israeli-Palestinian conflict and reconciliation, including lines about a child’s anti-war poem, soldiers in a pharmacy, and a bird whose wings cover two roofs.
counterfactuals.output:
Between the checkpoint and the olive tree  
a morning opens carefully,  
as if the sky itself  
has learned to knock before entering.

On one wall, a child has taped  
an anti-war poem in blue pencil:  
*I want the rockets to forget my street.  
I want the tanks to dream of being tractors.  
I want every mother to stop counting.*  

People read it in silence,  
then look away,  
ashamed of how small their prayers have become.

In the pharmacy, soldiers stand  
between cough syrup and bandages,  
their rifles dark against the shelves.  
An old man asks for medicine  
for a heart that will not sleep.  
The pharmacist lowers his voice  
as if peace might be startled  
and run.

Outside, two neighbors argue  
over a cracked water pipe,  
over names, over maps,  
over the dead who have become  
too many to carry  
and too sacred to set down.

Then, at dusk, a bird rises  
from the wire between houses,  
a bird whose wings cover two roofs—  
one with a satellite dish,  
one with a torn red kite,  
one family lighting candles,  
one family kneading bread.

For a moment, shadow joins them  
without asking permission.

No trumpet sounds.  
No treaty falls from heaven.  
Only a woman passing lemons  
over a broken fence,  
only a boy returning a lost shoe,  
only the pharmacy door still open  
after curfew,  
only the child’s poem  
lifting at the corners in the wind,

trying to become  
a flag no one has to die for.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a contemplative prose poem with the line “I’m not interested in who suffered the most. I’m interested in people getting over it,” blending tenderness, absurdity, political violence, and the possibility of forgiveness.
counterfactuals.output:
At the border, someone had planted marigolds in empty shell casings, and by morning the checkpoint smelled faintly of metal, rain, and stubborn yellow light.

A soldier with a child’s face waved us through with the same hand that had signed, or been told to sign, the papers for someone else’s disappearance. His boots were polished. His eyes were not. Behind him, a goat was chewing a campaign poster as if democracy were a difficult but edible weed.

No one laughed, so the goat did it for us.

There is a kind of tenderness that arrives late, wearing the wrong coat, carrying soup in a cracked pot. It does not know where to stand in a room full of survivors. It says foolish things. It touches the table, the doorframe, the back of a chair, as if asking permission from the furniture to remain.

“I’m not interested in who suffered the most. I’m interested in people getting over it,” said the woman whose brother had become a rumor in the prison system.

Then she sat down and fed orange slices to the man who had once informed on her family.

The room did not become holy. The dead did not return with clean shirts and apologies. Outside, loudspeakers coughed up another speech about unity, and somewhere a bureaucrat sharpened a pencil over a file marked unresolved. The nation continued, that ridiculous animal, limping on three legs and demanding applause.

But the man took the orange.

He wept incorrectly, with his mouth open, like a gate left swinging in the wind. The woman looked away, not out of mercy, exactly, but because mercy is too large a word for what the living can manage before lunch. She looked away because the kettle was boiling. Because someone had to slice bread. Because grief, after years of dictatorship, learns to perform small administrative tasks.

Forgiveness did not descend.

It wandered in sideways, smelling of onions, with a stain on its sleeve. It was not pardon, not forgetting, not the official photograph of former enemies planting a tree. It was more like allowing a cup to be refilled. More like refusing to become the shape the wound prescribed.

In the courtyard, the marigolds leaned toward the sun, absurd and obedient. The goat finished the candidate’s face and began on the slogan.

We stayed there a while, among the broken laws and citrus peels, listening to the kettle click itself quiet, each of us holding something hot we had not yet learned how to drink.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
